Professors Manuel Herrero-Puertas and Elizaveta (Lisa) Litovskaia teach, respectively, gothic literature & disability studies and Russian & social media/fan studies at National Taiwan University's Department of Foreign Languages and Literatures.

In this episode, they discuss:

  • 0:00–2:20: The Gothic in Taiwan 
  • 2:21–6:19: Vampires and vampire novels
  • 6:20–8:00: Professor Herrero-Puertas's Gothic Corporealities graduate seminar
  • 8:01–15:59: Fan studies, fandoms, fan practices, and studying these topics in academia
  • 16:00–19:41: Their research interests and how they developed
  • 19:42–27:16: Writing the (MA) thesis
  • 27:17–end: Reading recommendations for introductions to the Gothic, disability studies, and fan studies Prioritizing coursework and interests as a graduate student

Manuel Herrero-Puertas is an Associate Professor of Foreign Languages and Literatures at National Taiwan University, Taiwan, where he teaches courses on early and nineteenth-century American literature, disability studies, and the gothic. He writes on the intersection of literature, discourses of disability, neurodivergence, and horror.

His work has appeared in, among other venues, American Quarterly, Studies in American Fiction, Poe Studies, and the Journal of Literary & Cultural Disability Studies. His current monograph project argues for a non-psychoanalytic engagement with the transatlantic gothic, making a case instead for the genre’s accessible materiality and latent crip politics. 

Elizaveta Litovskaia is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Foreign Languages and Literatures at National Taiwan University, Taiwan. She teaches courses on Russian language and literature and graduate seminars on literature and fan reading practices on social media.

Her current research focuses on social media narratives about reading and literature, and on literature-related fandom practices in online communities. Previously, her work examined Russian and Soviet cookbooks from the nineteenth to the twenty-first centuries, exploring their connections to political, historical, and social contexts, as well as how these factors shape authors' self-presentation.

Professors Edward Nolan and Laurent Cases both teach Latin & Greek Classics at National Taiwan University's Department of Foreign Languages and Literatures.

In this episode, they discuss:

  • 1:34–4:17: Reactions to the promotional content of Christopher Nolan's film The Odyssey
  • 4:18–8:51: Researching the classics and finding what you want to research in grad school
  • 8:52–12:07: Preparation for graduate school (some of which is Classics-specific)
  • 12:08–16:30: The Latin program at NTU
  • 16:31–19:54: Latin at the graduate level
  • 19:55–21:20: Making Latin more accessible to graduate students who didn't study the Classics in their undergrad yeards
  • 21:21–22:24: Prioritizing coursework and interests as a graduate student

Edward Nolan is an Associate Professor of Classics in the Department of Foreign Languages and Literatures at National Taiwan University. He received a PhD in Classical Studies from the University of Michigan in 2021. A cultural historian and philologist, he researches ancient social thought, with a focus on ancient ideas about language. His current book project examines the Classical Greek historian Herodotus through a linguistic lens, revealing his engagement with other fifth-century BCE thinkers and his anticipation of modern linguistic concepts.
Laurent Cases is a historian of Late Antiquity, Late-Roman administration, institutions, and law, and currently an assistant professor of Classics in the Department of Foreign Languages and Literatures at the National Taiwan University, Taipei, Taiwan. He studied at the University of California, Santa Barbara (BA), the Institute for Medieval Studies at the University of Leeds (MA), and the Pennsylvania State University (MA/PhD), and was an ERC postdoctoral fellow in the faculty of Law at the University of Pavia. His work traces how the Roman Empire constructed its administrative apparatus and how this apparatus helped inform and transform cultural productions.
